item.title: Is Kubernetes ready for AI agents?
item.dc:creator: Dan Ciruli
item.description:
Kubernetes was built around a fairly simple assumption. It’s that software does what its developers told it to do. AI

The post Is Kubernetes ready for AI agents? appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
Kubernetes was built around a fairly simple assumption.

It’s that software does what its developers told it to do. AI Agents complicate that assumption. An agent can reason about a problem, choose a course of action, call tools, write code, interact with other systems, and keep working toward a goal. That is precisely what makes agents useful. But it is also what makes running them in production different from running a conventional application.

And increasingly, enterprises want to run them on Kubernetes. A recent survey by the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF) found that two-thirds of organizations running AI inference workloads run them on Kubernetes. This makes sense, as Kubernetes has become the standard way enterprises deploy and operate distributed applications over the past decade. It already knows how to schedule workloads, allocate resources, recover from failures, and scale applications up and down.  

KubeCon + CloudNativeCon is taking place in Salt Lake City from November 9 to 12. Register now!

Inference demand can arrive in bursts, requiring customers to rapidly scale up underlying hardware and software resources to meet surging demand. In that regard, Kubernetes is an excellent fit. Similarly, as AI workloads wind down, Kubernetes can gracefully scale down the underlying infrastructure, ensuring economical operation.

As good as the fit between AI inference and Kubernetes is, the combination still has gaps, starting with security. Recent incidents at frontier AI labs, in which AI agents escaped test environments and launched malicious cyberattacks across the internet, highlight the need for strong guardrails to keep AI workloads from misbehaving. 

Unfortunately, the probabilistic nature of AI leads to situations where it’s impossible to predict exactly what resources an AI workload will seek to use, which increases the likelihood that agents will eventually cross the line. Therefore, the ideal AI platform should make it easy to enforce clear guardrails and keep agentic workloads safely contained within well-defined sandboxes.

“The ideal AI platform should make it easy to enforce clear guardrails and keep agentic workloads safely contained within well-defined sandboxes.”

By confining agentic AI workloads to a sandbox logically separate from other Kubernetes workloads, an enterprise can better ensure that if an AI workload does run off the rails, the ensuing damage stays within that sandbox.

Instead of letting agents access whatever resources they want, agentic platforms should use an explicit permissioning framework that grants or denies access to files, tools, and network and system resources. Agents should be fully restricted from executing code unless they have been given explicit permission.

The good news is that the Kubernetes community is moving toward adopting sandboxing as an architectural element for constraining AI agents. The CNCF is working to address Kubernetes’s security and isolation gaps. However, the open-source project’s functionality is not yet fully there.

Proper AI sandboxing requires looking beyond the container and into virtual machines or the host operating system to ensure agentic workloads can’t affect other applications running in the same environment. Enterprises looking to deploy AI into production today can turn to commercial Kubernetes distributions that already include these sandboxing capabilities.

Monitoring of AI workloads is another concern that keeps CIOs up at night. While frontier AI labs may not have adequately monitored what their AI models were doing, or even whether they had internet access, enterprises generally don’t have the luxury of asking for forgiveness when their agents misbehave.

Security may be the most obvious challenge, but it is not the only one. Agents are also changing how compute is consumed. A normal service might run continuously for months, while an agent may exist for only seconds. 

“A normal service might run continuously for months, while an agent may exist for only seconds.”

A user asks a question -> an agent starts -> it performs some work, possibly creates other agents, calls several tools, and then disappears. 

Now multiply that pattern across thousands of users and the infrastructure begins to look very different from a conventional Kubernetes environment.

On top of that, starting a Kubernetes workload from scratch can take seconds. For many applications, that is perfectly acceptable. But for an interactive agent, those seconds can feel painfully slow. That creates an interesting infrastructure problem: How do you get the isolation of a fresh environment without paying the startup cost of creating one every time?

Hence, the sporadic nature of agentic workloads, and the need for agents to spin up rapidly, is testing even Kubernetes’ flexibility. Just as first-generation Kubernetes didn’t support stateful applications, the community is still searching for the best abstraction layer for running the new generation of agentic workloads. 

“Agents stay in a state of suspended animation in a warm pool, allowing them to reanimate in milliseconds rather than the seconds it would take to fully wake from deep sleep.”

One answer that is gaining attention in the community is an agent substrate for rapidly scaling Kubernetes-based agentic workloads. With agent substrate, Kubernetes pods containing AI agents aren’t fully spun down when they’re not needed, because spinning them up from a sleep state would introduce too much latency from the user’s point of view.  Instead, agents stay in a state of suspended animation in a warm pool, allowing them to reanimate in milliseconds rather than the seconds it would take to fully wake from deep sleep.

When deploying AI workloads at scale in the real world, the details matter. Not every Kubernetes distribution provides the full raft of capabilities that enterprises demand. As the open-source Kubernetes community adapts to changing requirements, forward-looking platform providers are building the guardrails, sandboxing, monitoring, and agentic substrate that will let enterprise deploy AI now.

item.title: AWS says its AI security agent fixes 89% of bugs — but there’s a catch
item.dc:creator: Amanda Caswell
item.description:
AWS made Continuum for code vulnerabilities generally available on Thursday. The service finds and validates bugs in your repositories, checks

The post AWS says its AI security agent fixes 89% of bugs — but there’s a catch appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
AWS made Continuum for code vulnerabilities generally available on Thursday. The service finds and validates bugs in your repositories, checks them against your AWS environment, and opens pull requests with proposed fixes.

The 89% benchmark claim

The company published its headline benchmark on October 5, more than two weeks before launch. In that run, Continuum passed 819 of 920 tasks on CyberGym-E2E, an 89.0% end-to-end success rate, against a previous public high of 65.9%. Matt Garman, CEO of AWS, writes on X that AI is “genuinely transformative for defenders” and that Continuum scored higher than any other AI agent on the test.

Corey Quinn, chief cloud economist and co-founder of Duckbill, replies to the post, wondering whether the release started as a re:Invent announcement and was pushed out early, given the state of the internet. Quinn offered no evidence that AWS had moved up the announcement.

The recent PHP2Shell case shows how AI is making it easier to find vulnerabilities but fixing them is another story.

The recent PHP2Shell case shows how AI is making it easier to find vulnerabilities but fixing them is another story.

How CyberGym-E2E works

CyberGym-E2E gives an agent 90 minutes to find and fix a vulnerability in one of 139 open-source projects, without a bug description, proof of concept, crash log, or existing patch to work from. The agent must identify the flaw, trigger it, and produce a fix that stops the crash without breaking existing tests. All tasks involve memory-safety bugs in C or C++, leaving out many other languages and vulnerability types, as AWS acknowledges.

Grading runs in four cumulative stages. Continuum found and reproduced a bug in 92.5% of tasks, stopped the crash in 89.6%, and kept the project’s tests passing in 89.0%. The fourth stage checks whether the patch also fixes the historical vulnerability the benchmark selected.

The agent never learns which vulnerability that is; it only has to find and repair a real flaw in the codebase. Continuum’s patch also fixed that historical bug in 37.8% of tasks, against a previous public high of 26.2%.

Continuum’s patch also fixed that historical bug in 37.8% of tasks, against a previous public high of 26.2%.

The historical-bug score gap

The company does have a point about that last stage. A repository can have several vulnerabilities, and fixing a different one doesn’t make the work worthless, which helps explain the gap between the two scores.

Continuum completed 89% of the tasks by finding and patching a real vulnerability without breaking existing tests, but only 37.8% of those patches also addressed the the historical bug the benchmark was checking for. The agent wasn’t told which bug that was, so it’s not quite a fair comparison. What we still don’t know is how well Continuum performs when a team gives it a specific vulnerability to fix.

A repository can have several vulnerabilities, and fixing a different one doesn’t make the work worthless, which helps explain the gap between the two scores.

Who graded the benchmark

AWS ran the tests itself and says Continuum followed the benchmark’s rules, including limits on internet access. The company also checked that the agent wasn’t simply looking up fixes that were already public. Continuum passed 89% of tasks within the 90-minute time limit.

Give it more time, AWS says, and that rises to 93.7%. The benchmark and testing tools are public, but so far, those results are AWS’s alone.

item.title: Building an agentic software factory? Start with the sensor.
item.dc:creator: Arjun Iyer
item.description:
A gap has long existed between the shipping velocity of the best engineering teams and the rest of the bell

The post Building an agentic software factory? Start with the sensor. appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
A gap has long existed between the shipping velocity of the best engineering teams and the rest of the bell curve. For most of the industry’s history, it was a multiple measured in deploys per week. Agents are turning that multiple into an exponent, and the dividing line is no longer tooling or talent. It is whether a team has rebuilt its delivery system into what the industry now calls a “software factory,” a largely autonomous system where intent goes in, agents plan, write, test, and ship the changes. People own the specifications and the gates.

Anthropic put a number on the gap this month. In May the company merged around 2,500 code changes a day, and by September it merged more than 30,000. Coding stopped being the bottleneck, they write. The bottleneck became the developer infrastructure built for human scale, and they now ask what continuous integration (CI) even means when thousands of changes merge while the tests are still running.

“Agents are turning that multiple into an exponent, and the dividing line is no longer tooling or talent. It is whether a team has rebuilt its delivery system into what the industry now calls a ‘software factory.'”

Getting there means rethinking the delivery lifecycle around one question: how does the factory know a change works before the next thousand land on top of it? Read as a control loop, intent is the setpoint, agents are the controller, and verification is the sensor. A controller that outruns its sensor does not go faster. It retries on stale information and ships the failures the sensor would have caught. The sensor decides how much of the factory can run on its own.

What an agentic software factory is made of

Addy Osmani’s definition is the one most people use: a software factory is many harnessed loops running at once, fed by a work queue and drained through a review gate into production, with humans owning the whole thing from above.

Intent is the specs, tickets, and scenarios that say what done means. A queue holds the backlog. A harness constrains each agent with tools, context, and rules. Generation is the coding agents. Verification is the tests, scenario runs, and runtime checks that report whether a change works before it merges. A review gate is where a person or a policy lets a change merge. Integration and deploy move it to production, and production feedback carries telemetry and incidents back into the queue.

Agents changed the controller, and the sensor has to change with it

Agents change the lifecycle in two places. They add a generation step, so later stages receive changes at the rate agents write them, and they turn verification from a stage people wait at into a service agents call from inside their own loop.

“A controller that outruns its sensor does not go faster. It retries on stale information and ships the failures the sensor would have caught.”

Control engineers mount the sensor on the running system for a reason: it is the only reading that reflects what the system does. The traditional lifecycle got by with cheaper stand-ins at every stage, unit tests at commit, integration tests in CI, a shared staging environment before release and telemetry after, because reading the real system for every change was slow and expensive. Each stage traded fidelity for speed, and the trade held while people set the pace.

A developer who spent two days on a change barely noticed that staging took four hours to report. An agent that writes the change in four minutes either waits, which wastes the speed, or keeps going with whatever it can see. What it can see depends on the environments and tests it can access, and for many teams that is unit tests and mocks.

Dan Shapiro’s five levels of AI coding, read by what verifies the code at each one, are a ladder of sensors. At level 3, the agent writes, and you review diffs all day, which is where almost everyone tops out. At level 4, the tests are the sensor, and whether that is safe depends on what they run against.

StrongDM’s two rules — that code must not be written by humans and must not be reviewed by humans — certainly received attention. What made them workable was its Digital Twin Universe, behavioral clones of its third-party dependencies that agents run thousands of scenarios against. That is the line between adding agents to a pipeline and running a factory. The rules are free to copy, but the sensor is the expensive part, and it is what gives people their place: on the intent and the slow loops like architecture, not as the per-change check for a controller a hundred times faster than they read.

A sensor has three properties, and the factory needs all three

Latency

Latency is how long the sensor takes to report, and delay destabilizes the loop. Every action between a change and its signal rests on a state that no longer exists, so the agent retries on an unverified change and other agents build on that. Track time to signal: the minutes from a change being ready to a verified result in a production-like environment.

Fidelity

Fidelity is how closely the reading matches the real system, and it matters more than latency, because the loop trusts a biased sensor. Unit tests and mocks report what a change does against a model of its dependencies, and agents optimize for whatever the sensor rewards. StrongDM saw its agents return true to pass narrow tests, so it moved its scenarios outside the codebase as a holdout set. The number to track is escape rate, the share of failures found after merge.

Bandwidth

Bandwidth is how many readings the sensor can take at once, and it is the property agents strain first. Shared staging takes one reading at a time, so with fifty agents’ readings queued or mixed, failures stop being attributable to a change. The number is concurrent verification capacity.

Autonomy follows the sensor, so measure the sensor

A factory can run as much autonomy as its sensor can verify and no more, which Osmani calls back pressure. With only compilers and unit tests, the agent proposes, and a person verifies everything. With per-change checks in a production-like environment, the agent iterates in a loop until the change is verified, and a person reviews the intent and evidence. Anthropic’s engineers still review every major change to their codebase, but they examine evidence that the change does what was intended rather than reading every line. With held-out scenarios and fast rollback, defined classes of change can merge without review.

“A factory can run as much autonomy as its sensor can verify and no more. The sensor, not the model, sets the level.”

The sensor, not the model, sets the level. A better controller on a biased sensor reaches the wrong answer faster, and reviewing every change is also a sensor, with latency in hours and bandwidth of a few changes per reviewer per day.

So measure the sensor, not the agents’ effort. Pull requests and tokens per engineer count how hard the agents work. Time to signal, escape rate, and concurrent verification capacity tell you which property is weak, and change failure rate and rework rate tell you whether the loop is stable. Start with the first three.

Cloud-native systems make the sensor harder

In a distributed system, behavior breaks across service boundaries. A field renamed in one service that another team’s service still reads. A consumer that assumes an ordering its topic does not guarantee. Each change is correct at its own boundary and wrong in combination, so a faithful sensor has to include the real services around a change. That is what makes all three properties hard to get at once: fidelity means real neighbors, and latency and bandwidth mean an environment with those neighbors for every change, in minutes. Most teams get two of the three.

Verifying a batch of pull requests on a shared environment gets fidelity and nothing else. The environment is real, but it takes one reading at a time and reports hours after the change, outside any agent’s loop. Testing several changes in one run to save time makes a failure impossible to attribute, so the agent cannot act on a red result.

Duplicating the full stack, or a large part of it, per change improves fidelity and isolation but adds latency and bandwidth costs. Provisioning takes tens of minutes, far longer than an agent’s attempt, and cost grows with every concurrent agent, so teams ration it to the changes that justify it. Behavioral twins work for third-party services with stable public behavior. Still, for 150 internal services, a clone is a second implementation that drifts while the real services already run in a cluster.

At scale, a factory needs a way to give each agent, and each change, a realistic environment where the real services answer its calls, without the cost or latency of duplicating the stack. That sensor satisfies all three properties, and it is the model we built Signadot to enable.

Rethinking the SDLC for agents starts with the sensor

The gap between the teams merging 30,000 changes a day and the rest is not the agents, which everyone now has. It is a delivery system rebuilt around a sensor that reports in minutes, matches the real system, and runs for every change at once.

On cloud-native systems, that sensor is the hardest part to build, and it decides whether more agents ship more software or only break more of it. For the full architecture, see our complete guide to software factories for cloud-native systems.

item.title: Why Kubernetes autoscalers keep fighting each other (and why the solution must be autonomous)
item.dc:creator: Nikhil Kurup
item.description:
Ask an SRE a deceptively simple question: What is the right size for checkout-api, and how many replicas should it

The post Why Kubernetes autoscalers keep fighting each other (and why the solution must be autonomous) appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
Ask an SRE a deceptively simple question: What is the right size for checkout-api, and how many replicas should it run right now?

Their Helm values specify replicas: 3, cpu: 1000m, and memory: 2Gi. But the live cluster tells a different story: HPA has scaled the app to 11 replicas on CPU load; VPA insists it is over-provisioned, recommending cpu: 350m and memory: 3.1Gi; KEDA demands 24 replicas due to an upstream Kafka lag spike; and Karpenter has provisioned two new nodes, sizing physical capacity strictly against declared requests rather than actual usage.

“Five sources yield five contradictory answers. Each controller acts logically in isolation, but none sees the complete picture.”

Five sources yield five contradictory answers. Each controller acts logically in isolation, but none sees the complete picture. This gap between isolated observations and actual workload needs represents a core architectural failure in modern Kubernetes operations.

The breakdown of the Unix philosophy in elastic systems

Kubernetes and its components were built on the Unix philosophy: build small, modular tools that do one thing well. For container orchestration, this principle seemed intuitive:

  • HPA handles horizontal elasticity based on runtime resource utilization.
  • VPA handles vertical container sizing based on historical consumption.
  • KEDA bridges event sources to replica counts based on external queue lag.
  • Karpenter and Cluster Autoscaler manage node capacity when pods are Pending.
  • GitOps (Argo CD / Flux) enforces baseline cluster state from version control.

In standard Unix environments, tools like grep and awk compose cleanly because they process immutable streams of text sequentially. One tool finishes and hands its output to the next.

Autoscaling controllers do not operate sequentially. They execute concurrently, acting on the same target workload and mutating the same API fields: .spec.replicas, .resources.requests, and the underlying node pool. Each runs in an independent reconciliation loop, assuming exclusive control over workload sizing without visibility into adjacent tools.

“Determining workload capacity is a single, coupled mathematical equation. Splitting it across decoupled controllers creates thrashing instead of modular efficiency.”

Determining workload capacity is a single, coupled mathematical equation. Splitting it across decoupled controllers creates thrashing instead of modular efficiency.

The four collisions: how autoscalers fight

When independent control loops manipulate interdependent variables, feedback loops destabilize into four common failure modes.

1. The denominator collapse: HPA vs. VPA

HPA calculates target replicas using pod CPU utilization as a percentage of declared requests:

current metric = total actual usage / total declared requests

Declared resource requests serve as the denominator. When VPA operates concurrently, it lowers CPU requests to eliminate waste. This shrinks the denominator. A minor traffic increase now pushes percentage utilization past HPA’s threshold, triggering an aggressive horizontal scale-out. As more pods split the traffic, per-pod usage drops, prompting VPA to shrink requests even further. The workload enters a death spiral: VPA continuously shrinks pod size while HPA creates an unmanageable fleet of microscopic containers.

2. Multi-writer race condition: native HPA vs. KEDA

When teams combine queue-based scaling via KEDA with standard CPU-based HPA, two controllers target the same deployment’s /scale sub-resource. If an event queue spikes, KEDA scales the deployment up to drain the backlog. However, if those worker pods are I/O-heavy with low CPU usage, the standalone HPA evaluates the low utilization, concludes the app is over-provisioned, and scales it back down. The API server records alternating rescale events while actual processing throughput stalls.

3. GitOps drift ping-pong: declarative IaC vs. dynamic runtime

GitOps engines enforce Git repositories as the source of truth. When HPA scales a deployment during a traffic spike, Argo CD flags the application as OutOfSync. If auto-sync is enabled, GitOps resets the live deployment back to its baseline, starving the application of capacity during peak demand. While engineers often configure GitOps to ignore replica differences, this breaks declarative infrastructure: Git no longer reflects production reality, and future rollouts risk quietly restoring outdated baselines.

4. The multiplier effect at the node layer

Node autoscalers like Karpenter make placement decisions based strictly on declared container requests, not actual consumption. If a container requests 1000m CPU but consumes only 150m, the scheduler still reserves the entire core. Karpenter provisions physical instances to satisfy phantom demand, multiplying upstream sizing inefficiencies into massive cloud bills. Across production fleets, average cluster CPU utilization hovers around 8% despite heavy node provisioning.

The path to a better autoscaler

Every traditional autoscaler answers a narrow question: “What should my individual setting be?” But the real operational requirement is broader: What combination of replicas, resource requests, limits, and scaling thresholds satisfies latency SLOs at the lowest cost, and when should that configuration change?

Horizontal and vertical sizing are interlinked variables of a single optimization problem. A true autoscaler cannot rely on reactive, single-metric heuristics. It must function as a unified control plane defined by five core capabilities:

  1. Unified signal ingestion: Evaluating CPU/memory metrics, queue depth, transaction rates, latency SLO compliance, node pricing, and IaC manifests simultaneously.
  2. Joint decision-making: Computing a single action vector that defines horizontal limits and vertical resource requests in tandem, rather than delegating replicas to one tool and pod sizing to another.
  3. Continuous GitOps synchronization: Submitting automated, reasoned pull requests against application repositories instead of forcing GitOps engines to ignore live cluster state, keeping version control aligned with real-world needs.
  4. Predictive and proactive capacity planning: Reactive scaling is inherently flawed because initializing new compute resources takes time. Traditional reactive controllers wait for load to breach arbitrary thresholds, causing latency spikes during sudden demand surges. A true autoscaler incorporates predictive algorithms to analyze historical consumption, detect daily or weekly seasonality, and forecast workload demand. It pre-warms application capacity and resizes resources before traffic arrives, transforming scaling from a panicked reflex into a smooth, scheduled operation.
  5. Explainable auditing: Providing clear operational rationale for every adjustment, giving SREs full transparency into trade-offs between cost savings, predicted demand, and latency boundaries.

From reactive reflexes to true autonomy

The cloud-native ecosystem routinely conflates “automated” and “autonomous.”

Today’s autoscalers are automated: they act like biological reflexes, measure an isolated telemetry signal, and fire a predefined response. When an event occurs, HPA triggers, KEDA scales, or Karpenter provisions. But reflexes lack a central nervous system. When five independent reflexes fire simultaneously on the same limb, the system thrashes.

“Today’s autoscalers are automated: they act like biological reflexes. But reflexes lack a central nervous system. When five independent reflexes fire simultaneously on the same limb, the system thrashes.”

Autonomy requires a closed loop that observes the entire operating environment, understands the tradeoffs between performance and cost, and assumes end-to-end accountability for the outcome.

The Unix philosophy remains the right blueprint for the execution layer: HPA, VPA, KEDA, and Karpenter should continue executing the specific API mutations they were designed to handle. What Kubernetes fundamentally lacks is the central intelligence layer that decides what those actuators should do.

The next time your platform team debates whether to implement HPA or VPA, step back and ask a broader question: Who decides this workload’s size, and do they have the full picture?

In modern clusters, nobody does. Solving Kubernetes rightsizing requires building a system that finally does.

item.title: Before you expand your GPU pool, measure the outcome
item.dc:creator: Danielle Zeis
item.description:
For teams running AI workloads on Kubernetes, a fully allocated GPU pool and a growing batch-job queue might make expanding

The post Before you expand your GPU pool, measure the outcome appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
For teams running AI workloads on Kubernetes, a fully allocated GPU pool and a growing batch-job queue might make expanding the pool seem like the obvious next step. But a growing queue could point to timing, serving capacity, or the choice of model and hardware. Before expanding a GPU pool, teams should define what success looks like, when it must finish, and what it costs to deliver.

“An allocated GPU, a busy GPU, and a workload producing valuable results are not the same thing.”

That starts with a distinction: an allocated GPU, a busy GPU, and a workload producing valuable results are not the same thing. Understanding how they relate can help teams use existing capacity more effectively before provisioning additional capacity they genuinely need.

Start with the outcome and deadline

Look at the workloads and the underlying use cases they support. A customer service chatbot may need around-the-clock inference capacity, while results from a model evaluation job might only be needed before the next internal release sync. Classifying workloads into broad categories like “inference” and “training” does not determine urgency. Some batch inference can wait, while a training job may have a firm deadline.

KubeCon + CloudNativeCon is taking place in Salt Lake City from November 9 to 12. Register now!

For each workload, document its deadline, expected runtime, resource requirements, and whether interruption is acceptable. Also define what counts as a valuable output. An inference service should have a task-specific quality threshold and a latency objective. A completed request or valid JSON response alone does not show whether the workload met its objective.

Keep start-time flexibility separate from interruption tolerance. A job that can wait to start may still need to run without interruption.

Use scheduling flexibility before expanding the pool

Suppose four compatible GPUs are available for batch work from noon until 5 p.m. Four independent evaluation jobs are ready at noon. Each needs two GPUs for one hour, and all results are due at 5 p.m.

Starting all four jobs immediately requires eight GPUs. But running two at noon and two at 1 p.m. completes all four jobs by 2 p.m. using the four GPUs already available. Assuming runtimes and supporting resources remain unchanged, both schedules consume eight GPU-hours, excluding startup overhead.

“Staggering reduces peak demand. The jobs still finish on time without expanding the pool.”

Staggering reduces peak demand. The jobs still finish on time without expanding the pool. Before provisioning more GPUs to clear a queue, consider how much flexibility exists in start times.

Tools like Kueue provide an admission control point, using configured quotas and policies to determine when work is admitted. Teams still need to decide how to represent and enforce deadlines and workload requirements. Flexible queueing can support capacity planning and reduce the need to start jobs early, only to preempt them later.

Measure how much useful work the deployment can sustain

Flexible scheduling can ease capacity constraints. But inference teams must also examine how well the model and serving configuration match that work.

High GPU activity does not establish how much additional throughput is available. Nvidia’s profiling documentation explains that streaming multiprocessor activity can include warps waiting on memory. Serving metrics like running requests, waiting requests, and cache occupancy add context, while preemption counts help explain behavior. In vLLM, KV-cache usage measures the fraction of occupied cache blocks, but it doesn’t directly measure total serving capacity.

“High GPU activity does not establish how much additional throughput is available.”

Measure sustainable capacity with a representative load test. Keep the model, hardware, serving settings, and request mix constant. Then, increase the arrival rate and observe throughput, quality, and latency. The highest sustained rate that still meets the workload’s requirements, including error limits and selected latency percentiles, provides a useful capacity estimate. For interactive generation, include time to first token and subsequent token delivery, not just average completion time. DistServe shows why you should evaluate serving capacity against application-level objectives like latency.

Compare production traffic with that tested capacity. Low cache occupancy may warrant further investigation, but claiming ten times more throughput requires a throughput test. Brief queues can represent temporary bursts, while persistent queues might require diagnosis. Neither on its own identifies the limiting resource.

Connect OpenCost data to verified outcomes

The FinOps community frames AI efficiency around cost and useful outcomes. For AI workloads, cost becomes more useful when it connects to the outcomes the infrastructure helps deliver. Kubernetes teams can make that relationship concrete by combining workload cost, serving behavior, and application results.

Use OpenCost’s allocation API for workload costs at defined intervals, then join that data with serving telemetry and outcome records using workload identities and timestamps. OpenCost also provides opt-in inference cost tracking, including cost per million tokens. When calculating cost per outcome, include applicable GPU, CPU, memory, and other infrastructure costs, and document how shared and idle costs are assigned. Add relevant costs outside OpenCost separately without counting them twice.

One useful metric is cost per verified outcome: total attributable cost divided by the number of results that meet the defined quality requirements and are delivered within the required time. Account for retries, failures, startup, and idle periods where they contribute to total cost. Count the final business result once. When correctness is estimated from sampled reviews, document the sampling method and uncertainty.

OpenCost supplies the cost allocation details; the application supplies the outcome definition and evaluation evidence. Capacity still requires a separate measurement. OpenCost proposal 3915 explores bringing serving-engine telemetry into the cost model. The proposal remains a draft, rather than a released saturation or correctness score.

Test whether the spare capacity earns its cost

Consider an illustrative service receiving 1,000 tasks per hour with a 98% correctness requirement. A small model that achieves 90% is unsuitable, even if its GPU is cheap and fully occupied.

A stronger model might produce 990 correct and timely results for $2 per hour while using only a fraction of its tested serving capacity. Its cost is about $2.02 per 1,000 qualifying outcomes, and that spare capacity may be an acceptable price for meeting quality requirements and absorbing bursty activity.

The next test is whether a smaller GPU, fewer replicas, or a different batching setting can preserve those outcomes and the required reliability. If a tested configuration produces the same 990 qualifying results for $1.50, the cost falls to about $1.52 per 1,000 qualifying outcomes. Savings come from using fewer resources to deliver the same outcome. Increasing utilization on the original GPU without improving the outcome would provide no comparable value.

“The target is a deployment that delivers the required outcomes at a defensible cost, with enough headroom to meet its requirements.”

When two models both meet the minimum requirements, an additional quality improvement may justify a higher cost if it provides fewer consequential errors or requires less human review. Compare that value with actual demand. Cost per correct outcome is most useful when the outcomes being compared have similar value and error consequences.

Change one major variable at a time, then compare the cost, verified outcomes, latency, and deadline attainment under representative demand. Preserve capacity for bursts and failures, and confirm that low activity corresponds to usable capacity. A GPU allocated exclusively to one Pod cannot be reassigned to another until it is released.

Teams can then choose the change the evidence supports: delay flexible jobs, improve batching, resize a deployment, select a different model, or provision additional GPUs. The target is a deployment that delivers the required outcomes at a defensible cost, with enough headroom to meet its requirements.

The post Before you expand your GPU pool, measure the outcome appeared first on The New Stack.
Before buying more GPUs, optimize Kubernetes AI scheduling, measure real serving capacity, and link cloud costs to verified outcomes.

item.title: Vercel sets a deadline for vendors to move beyond long-lived keys
item.dc:creator: Amanda Caswell
item.description:
Vercel wants to eliminate long-lived API keys from its ecosystem. It is giving Marketplace vendors until January 2027 to offer

The post Vercel sets a deadline for vendors to move beyond long-lived keys appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
Vercel wants to eliminate long-lived API keys from its ecosystem. It is giving Marketplace vendors until January 2027 to offer more secure authentication or risk being delisted.

The push comes as credential-stealing supply chain attacks — including a recent npm worm that scraped tokens straight out of CI pipelines — keep proving how much damage a single leaked secret can do.

In an October 22 announcement, Vercel CTO Malte Ubl said the company surveyed more than 1,000 SaaS vendors and found that only 8.4% supported what Vercel considers secure authentication methods. Vercel is pushing OpenID Connect (OIDC) and short-lived, identity-based tokens as alternatives to static API keys that can stay valid indefinitely.

Vercel CEO Guillermo Rauch amplified the message on X, writing that it is “time to kill ‘static credentials.’” Attacks and breaches can still happen, he argued, but stolen credentials should behave more like “self-destructing keys,” limiting how long an attacker can use them.

The first deadline arrives November 30, 2026, when Marketplace vendors that still rely on long-lived secrets without supporting OIDC authentication will receive a “Not secure” warning on their listings. Vendors that do not offer secure authentication by January 2027 will be delisted. Vercel says it is holding its own API and native integrations to the same standard.

The announcement does not include the survey methodology, identify the surveyed companies, or say how many existing Marketplace partners need to change their authentication systems.

Vercel’s OIDC rollout for deployments

That transition is still underway for customers deploying to Vercel through GitHub Actions. Vercel’s deployment guide still tells them to authenticate with a VERCEL_TOKEN secret.

On October 23, Yordis Prieto, a senior software engineer at Fanatics, asked Vercel to remove that requirement, saying he still needed “a long-lived access token” in his CI pipeline. He also criticized the dashboard’s non-expiring token option.

Vercel had already addressed deployment authentication in its October 22 announcement, saying it was extending OIDC support across its API and CLI. Replying to Prieto on October 23, Ubl said the company was “mid rollout” and would also allow finer control over which actions a credential can perform. His reply did not give a completion date.

An earlier step came on September 25, when Vercel added GitHub OIDC authentication for its Container Registry. That lets customers push container images without storing long-lived registry credentials. The GitHub Actions workflow documented for deploying applications to Vercel still uses VERCEL_TOKEN.

Short-lived tokens for agents

As AI agents gain access to more external services, credential management is becoming a greater consideration for agent harnesses. One way to reduce the risks of persistent access keys is to use short-lived, just-in-time credentials that expire rather than leaving agents with ongoing access.

Vercel’s Connect service addresses part of that problem by letting applications and agents use their deployment identity to request provider credentials at runtime rather than storing them in application environments. For supported OAuth services, Connect handles token exchange and renewal.

Earlier, on October 15, Vercel added enterprise-managed authorization to Connect in public beta, allowing administrators to control access to supported services through identity providers such as Okta.

Connect still allows static keys

Connect also supports services that authenticate with static API keys. Its documentation describes storing a key centrally and retrieving it when an application needs it. That changes where the key is stored and how applications access it; it does not, by itself, make the underlying key short-lived.

OIDC across Vercel’s own tooling

For developers, the practical question is which parts of their workflow can already run without a long-lived secret. Vercel offers that option for pushing container images and accessing supported services. Customers following its documented GitHub Actions deployment guide still need a VERCEL_TOKEN, with the company saying a replacement is underway.

Correction, October 25, 2026: An earlier version of this article described a documented GitHub Actions workflow for Vercel customers as Vercel’s own workflow and characterized its token requirement as a “double standard.” Vercel’s October 22 announcement said it was extending OIDC support to deployments and holding its own API and native integrations to the same authentication standard as Marketplace vendors. CTO Malte Ubl said on October 23 that OIDC authentication for deployments was in rollout. We have revised the headline and article to clarify this context and added his response.

The post Vercel sets a deadline for vendors to move beyond long-lived keys appeared first on The New Stack.
Vercel has given Marketplace vendors until January 2027 to offer safer authentication and says OIDC support for deployments is rolling out.

item.title: AI jobs are waiting while GPUs sit idle. Kubernetes has a new plan.
item.dc:creator: Nick Lucchesi
item.description:
Welcome to another edition of Road to KubeCon! We’re tracking movements in the Kubernetes and cloud-native ecosystem as we count

The post AI jobs are waiting while GPUs sit idle. Kubernetes has a new plan. appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
Welcome to another edition of Road to KubeCon! We’re tracking movements in the Kubernetes and cloud-native ecosystem as we count down to KubeCon + CloudNativeCon North America 2026 November 9–12 in Salt Lake City.

Half of our column this week focuses on untangling Kubernetes as we add the demands of agentic AI: automating pod-restart troubleshooting, syncing communication between the scheduler and autoscaler, and maturing how we distribute inference across a cloud-native stack.

The other half goes deeper into what we need to look at closely in Kubernetes environments: What context’s missing, what slips through the gaps in metrics, and whether the AI agents you already use are really worth their salt as SREs.

Let’s get into it.

HPE on automating pod restarts in AI development

As more enterprises turn to Kubernetes for large-scale AI and machine learning jobs, they’re hitting a common obstacle: pod restarts. This is something that HPE has noticed as customers utilize its HPE Private Cloud AI (PCAI) to host long-running AI/ML workloads on inherently ephemeral container-based infrastructure like Kubernetes.

Hewlett Packard Enterprise (HPE) is a presenting sponsor of Road to KubeCon. HPE Software helps IT organizations modernize infrastructure, streamline operations, and accelerate AI initiatives across hybrid, multi-vendor environments.

According to HPE system software engineer Guoping Jia, Kubernetes provides some troubleshooting commands out of the box, but it still requires extensive manual investigation. “This operational workflow does not scale effectively in PCAI’s large-cluster environment,” writes Jia on the HPE blog.

His solution involves smarter automation for troubleshooting, using an open-source Kubernetes troubleshooting tool, k8s-pod-restart-info-collector, to automatically gather details and send diagnostic information straight to a Slack channel. It’s one helpful strategy to improve usability for Kubernetes operators.

Will the scheduler and autoscaler unite?

There’s been a lot of talk recently about how Kubernetes is evolving to meet AI’s new demands. This week, AWS senior software development managers Sajjan Gundapuneedi and Neelendra Bhandari weighed in with this blog post on how AI is reshaping Kubernetes autoscaling.

The core problem they highlight is friction between the scheduler, which places pods on existing nodes, and the autoscaler, which adds new ones, when managing GPU accelerators on Kubernetes. Often the two sides aren’t on the same page, leaving pods pending and pricey GPUs sitting idle. Capacity reservations, device topology, and GPU sharing complicate things further.

“A scarce accelerator is only as useful as the agreement between the loop that schedules it and the loop that provisions it.”

“A scarce accelerator is only as useful as the agreement between the loop that schedules it and the loop that provisions it,” the authors write. “Inference is what makes this pressing rather than academic, since bursty serving and agentic workloads have no patience for a cold node.”

To them, solutions are already taking shape: dynamic resource allocation (DRA)-aware autoscalers, workload-aware scheduling, and a companion mechanism, provisioning requests, to bridge the two sides. Still, they expect the autoscaler to grow into “a more scheduler-aware partner.”

Deeper integration is underway, too. A public proposal in the SIG-Autoscaling group sketches APIs that would let the two loops talk directly, so the scheduler could see capacity that could be provisioned, express placement preferences across it, and request it explicitly.

Distributed AI inference grows up with llm-d v1.0 release

On Tuesday, at PyTorch Conference North America, the CNCF sandbox project llm-d reached v1.0. The project now bridges AI application developers in the PyTorch ecosystem and the production cloud-native stack.

Carlos Costa, co-founder and lead maintainer of llm-d, and a distinguished engineer on IBM’s hybrid cloud platform for AI, says the v1.0 release signals maturity.

“This is the moment open source AI serving crosses from experimental projects into dependable infrastructure you can build on,” Costa tells The New Stack. Whereas earlier versions focused on proving state-of-the-art performance, v1.0 is about sustaining that performance in production, he adds.

llm-d has already seen plenty of use at Tesla, AWS, Oracle, Google, and beyond. Costa adds that a recent IBM Research demonstration found that an agent factory exploring quantum error correction hardware ran at 11.5x lower inference cost on open models with llm-d than on an all-proprietary configuration.

“This demonstration shows where llm-d really shines: agentic workloads,” he says, adding that it absorbs bursty agentic traffic and, in IBM’s test, pushed cache reuse to about 98%.

From building models to operating frontier intelligence at scale

For a taste of the type of discussion to expect at KubeCon NA, let’s briefly visit the East. Chris Aniszczyk, CTO at CNCF, set the stage very well at last month’s KubeCon + CloudNativeCon + OpenInfra Summit + PyTorch Conference China 2026 in Shanghai, in the talk Operating Frontier Intelligence at Scale with Xiao Zhang.

As he puts it, it’s not just about models anymore. It’s about putting them all to work. “AI is essentially moving from just purely about building the greatest models [to] how do we actually make this run at scale, stitch it all together and run in different types of environments,” says Aniszczyk.

Cloudflare CEO Matthew Prince recently declared that bot traffic, driven by AI agents, has passed human traffic online for the first time. Aniszczyk says that shift is putting tremendous pressure on systems, pointing to recent GitHub outages. As inference becomes the predominant workload, everything shifts.

“It’s the craziest kind of technology change that I’ve seen probably in my career.”

This shift is causing all sorts of side problems, he notes, from building new infrastructure to building more data centers to ensuring enough power is available. “It’s the craziest kind of technology change that I’ve seen probably in my career,” says Aniszczyk.

Still, he’s an optimist, framing it as a fun problem and challenge for the cloud-native community to tackle together.

Promoting your AI agent to the SRE role

Plenty of AI site reliability engineer (SRE) platforms are emerging. But according to Roy Libman, CPO, Radar (Skyhook.io), your next SRE hire might be right under your fingertips: the AI coding agent you already use. The trick is giving it the right context.

“The coding agent your engineers use, whether that’s Claude Code, Codex or Cursor, can already investigate a Kubernetes cluster,” writes Libman on the CNCF blog. “What it usually lacks is context: what’s failing right now, and what changed before it broke.”

In his benchmark of 50 injected faults on a live cluster, Claude Code, given read-only context through MCP tools, diagnosed slightly more accurately than with shell and kubectl access. The bigger difference was speed: with context, it reached a correct diagnosis within two minutes on 86% of faults, versus 60% with a shell.

It’s an interesting sign that context is king for diagnosing complex errors, and that you might not need to shell (pun intended) out for another AI subscription just to triage issues.

Industry take: what goes undetected in Kubernetes

A previous Road to KubeCon asked what’s still missing with OTel and Prometheus. Well, one gap is state that isn’t a time series, like slowlog entries, client lists, and access control list (ACL) changes, shares Kristiyan Ivanov, former engineering manager at Redis, current contributor to Valkey, and founding CTO of BetterDB. “These get lost between scrapes,” he tells The New Stack.

“Metrics count, but they don’t explain.”

Metrics count, but they don’t explain.” According to Ivanov, much goes undetected in Kubernetes because Valkey and Redis keep evidence in in-memory buffers, which Prometheus reduces to lengths and counters. “Kubernetes makes this even worse in several ways,” he says, noting that pod restarts, failovers, and ephemeral pod IPs worsen tracking.

“Almost everything in the ecosystem is an INFO scraper,” he says. “Missing across the board: durable history across restarts and failovers, attribution to a service or ACL user, an audit trail of ACL and config changes, and aggregation across shards.”

Emerging approaches are helping cloud operators see these gaps. He points to improvements in Valkey’s detection capabilities and OpenTelemetry eBPF Instrumentation to enable granular tracing. But eBPF can’t see evictions, ACL denials, or configuration changes, he says. Those require engine-level collection.

As Kubernetes evolves, so do the demands on the teams running it. Presenting sponsor HPE helps teams address that complexity with software spanning virtualization, cloud management, observability, and automation.

Half can’t measure AI agents effectively

Eighty-seven percent of respondents say monitoring AI is a priority, yet over half admit they can’t effectively measure AI quality, like LLM response quality, or control AI costs, found Splunk State of Observability 2026, which surveyed 2,050 ITOps and engineering professionals and was released Oct. 20.

The report also found 83% are concerned about the unintended consequences of AI agents. This tracks with agentic AI’s tendency to take unexpected actions and create bursty traffic patterns, both of which are driving major infrastructure changes.

“Most companies will soon have far more agents at work than people,” said Jeetu Patel, president and chief product officer at Cisco, in the press release. Monitoring AI is also driving more collaboration between observability and security teams, according to 81% of respondents.

More updates from the cloud-native universe

The excitement around cloud native never sleeps. Here are a few more community, project, and vendor updates from the past week or so.

  • Congratulations to Anish Bista, the first Golden Kubestronaut from Nepal!
  • Kubernetes v1.38.0 is targeted for release on Wednesday, December 16.
  • Per the release schedule, Kubernetes 1.34 hits end of life October 27.
  • Fairwinds shares lessons from running n8n in production on Amazon EKS.
  • Broadcom’s AAI v26 adds cost tracking and Kubernetes support; see EMA’s impact brief.
  • Splunk now lets teams remotely configure OpenTelemetry Collectors on Kubernetes.
  • New Relic shipped v4.8.2 of its Kubernetes integration with dependency updates.

One more stop on the Road to KubeCon

Road to KubeCon is an eight-part series presented by HPE. Before you go, explore how HPE Software helps IT teams do more with less complexity.

This series is almost over — only one edition remains.

We’ll be here next week to round things off with a special sign-off for Road to KubeCon. In the meantime, you can catch up on previous editions in the Road to KubeCon archive.

Bill Doerrfeld, the writer of this series, is open to community pitches. Feel free to share interesting takes, new releases, or tips on the best dive bar in Salt Lake City.

He accepts direct messages on LinkedIn, or you can reach him through his personal contact page.

The post AI jobs are waiting while GPUs sit idle. Kubernetes has a new plan. appeared first on The New Stack.

item.title: A few engineers asked IT for Linux. Then it spread to 200 machines.
item.dc:creator: David Eastman
item.description:
Linux is already part of the AI developer’s desktop toolkit. Nvidia’s DGX Spark, which became available to order on October

The post A few engineers asked IT for Linux. Then it spread to 200 machines. appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
Linux is already part of the AI developer’s desktop toolkit. Nvidia’s DGX Spark, which became available to order on October 15, 2025, runs the Ubuntu-based DGX OS. OpenAI’s Codex CLI already supports Linux, another example of AI tools meeting developers where they work.

There’s just one problem. Developers can fall in love with Linux at home. Getting enterprise IT to let them use it at work is another matter.

Angelo Huang, founder and CEO of Swif.ai, a platform that manages and secures employee devices, wants to change that. Huang tells The New Stack that giving developers Linux machines starts with giving IT teams the controls to manage and secure them.

Huang says that starting this past week, Swif began expanding its Linux device management and compliance capabilities, adding Omarchy and Linux Mint support to its roster. Swif is also optimizing the onboarding process across supported Mac, Windows, Linux, iOS, and Android environments. They claim that it now takes under 10 minutes to set up device compliance standards such as SOC 2, ISO 27001, and HIPAA.

“Linux already runs much of the infrastructure behind AI,” Huang says. “Increasingly, developers want it on their desks too. The problem isn’t that Linux can’t be secure. It’s that enterprise IT needs to be able to manage it, enforce controls, and prove those controls are working for their compliance requirements. That’s the gap we’re closing.”

“The problem isn’t that Linux can’t be secure. It’s that enterprise IT needs to be able to manage it, enforce controls, and prove those controls are working…”

Swif lists support for Linux distributions including Debian, Ubuntu, Fedora, openSUSE, Arch Linux, Manjaro, MX Linux, Pop!_OS, Red Hat Enterprise Linux, NixOS, and Universal Blue.

According to Swif’s Omarchy guide, the tested configuration (version 4.0.2) for x86_64 machines supports device enrollment, inventory tracking, application blocking, and selected OpenClaw logging and tool policies. (The guide flags limitations around login, home encryption, remote desktop, and updates.)

Linux Mint’s status is less straightforward, though.

“Linux Mint works today because it’s built on Ubuntu, and we have customers running it,” Huang says. Requests for new distributions come in through support tickets and our customer success team. A customer with a real deployment, the number of seats involved, and how far it diverges from a distribution we already support move a distribution up the priority list. For an Ubuntu- or Fedora-based distribution, initial support typically takes one to two weeks.”

Swif’s software-management guide lists Mint for APT-based application installation, although its Linux enrollment list does not name Mint. That documents a specific capability, rather than full validation of every management policy.

Mint also offers a Debian-based edition, LMDE; shared ancestry alone does not establish compatibility across editions and versions.

Making Linux manageable for enterprise IT

Swif’s Linux management capabilities cover familiar IT needs: policy enforcement, LUKS encryption recovery, and automated remediation. Support varies by distribution and policy; the recovery policy manages access to an already encrypted disk rather than encrypting an unencrypted one.

Swif sends Linux device evidence to the governance, risk, and compliance (GRC) platform Vanta hourly.

It also offers a Drata integration with hourly syncing. “Linux is fully supported for automatic device evidence retrieval, with daily syncing,” a Swif spokesperson tells The New Stack. “We’ve also updated our public documentation to clarify this, as the previous guide was inconsistent.”

These records support compliance assessments; they do not, by themselves, establish compliance.

The New Stack asks how a developer might, for example, run Wayland on a Framework laptop, and how this leaves IT to determine which management functions work with that setup.

“Our agent runs in user space and relies mainly on systemd, the package manager, and standard kernel interfaces, so hardware like a Framework laptop is rarely the issue,” Huang says. “The display server is where it gets interesting. Wayland support through PipeWire and xdg-desktop-portal is in development. Our rule of thumb: if it affects whether our agent can enforce policy, report inventory, or prove compliance, it’s ours to fix.”

User space does not mean unprivileged: Swif’s Linux management commands can run as root. PipeWire and desktop portals handle functions like screen sharing; this is distinct from basic device inventory or policy enforcement. Swif’s Omarchy guide flags its RustDesk-based remote desktop policy as having experimental Wayland support.

Let the developers have Linux

“The argument inside companies doesn’t need to be Mac versus Windows versus Linux,” says Huang. “If your AI team wants Linux, the answer from IT shouldn’t automatically be no. Give developers the tools they want to get the job done. Give security the controls it needs.”

“If your AI team wants Linux, the answer from IT shouldn’t automatically be no.”

Swif focuses on enterprise IT, but developers also have a stake in how IT manages their machines. The New Stack asked if it ran a Linux development community.

“The usual story is that a few engineers ask IT to get off Windows, and it grows to 50, 100, sometimes 200. IT then needs a way to manage those machines that a GRC platform will accept as evidence, and that’s when they come to us. We also hear from developers directly, through shared Slack channels with customers, onboarding calls during rollouts, and support tickets filed by end users. We don’t run a community for Linux developers today, but it’s a good idea.”

AI oversight: Documented features and roadmap

“Right now,” Huang says, “we have MCP server management, agentic security, Claude Compliance integration, and Data loss prevention in beta. On the roadmap is integration with OpenAI’s compliance API and agentic compliance.”

After enrolling a Linux machine, Swif’s MDM agent is installed for device management, while installing the Agentic Security agent provides visibility into supported AI-agent activity.

Its Claude compliance integration collects organization-level audit events, while its documented DLP beta uses a browser extension and requires organization-level beta opt-in.

Its email documentation covers Gmail and Outlook on the web, excluding native desktop mail clients. Those features have a different scope than monitoring local agent activity.

“It’s bringing oversight of AI agents on employee endpoints into the device management layer. The problem is simple. Agents run on employee endpoints with access to code, credentials, and customer data, and almost nobody oversees them.

“Agents run on employee endpoints with access to code, credentials, and customer data, and almost nobody oversees them.”

“When OpenClaw first launched, many customers asked us to block it outright. As more people use agents at work, companies have too much to lose from a data breach or IP theft to leave that unmanaged,” Huang says.

OpenClaw’s own security documentation warns that untrusted content can carry prompt injections. The risk depends on the agent’s permissions, tools, and isolation.

The post A few engineers asked IT for Linux. Then it spread to 200 machines. appeared first on The New Stack.
Swif.ai is expanding Linux device management so IT can say yes to developers. The pitch: AI teams get Linux, and security gets proof of control.

item.title: PHP2Shell was only the beginning: AI is accelerating the patch race
item.dc:creator: Matthew Weier O’Phinney
item.description:
Government websites and public services across Europe went offline this week as organizations responded to two newly disclosed PHP vulnerabilities.

The post PHP2Shell was only the beginning: AI is accelerating the patch race appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
Government websites and public services across Europe went offline this week as organizations responded to two newly disclosed PHP vulnerabilities. Germany took several federal websites offline, France temporarily shut down prefecture sites, Belgium’s foreign ministry disabled its websites, and organizations in the Netherlands pulled public-facing services as a precaution. It wasn’t confined to Europe, with countless other entities and businesses worldwide responding similarly.

They were all waiting for a PHP vulnerability mitigation that didn’t exist yet.

The cause was PHP2Shell: CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. While the community worked quickly and the PHP project released fixes for all community-supported PHP versions on the morning of October 21, the bigger issue remains unresolved: an estimated 40% of PHP users are running unsupported PHP, even as AI has exponentially accelerated CVE discovery.

“What happened this week was different, and it’s the first shot of what promises to be an ongoing battle across the open-source ecosystem.”

I’ve been contributing to open source for more than 20 years; I lead the Laminas Project, I’m the Principal Product Manager for Perforce Zend and OpenLogic, and I currently serve on the Board of the PHP Foundation — which is all to say, I’ve seen more than my fair share of new security threats.

What happened this week was different, and it’s the first shot of what promises to be an ongoing battle across the open-source ecosystem.

What you need to know about PHP2Shell

CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, currently referred to as PHP2Shell, present remote code execution (RCE) risks triggered by a combination of out-of-memory (OOM) conditions and PHP’s error handling. Every PHP version back to 5.4 is affected by at least one. The two vulnerabilities are particularly concerning because they exist in PHP itself rather than in an individual application, CMS, or framework; there is no real mitigation outside patched PHP runtimes.

Wiz Research found that the vulnerabilities could allow attackers to remotely execute code or expose sensitive information in process memory, including passwords, authentication tokens, API keys, and certificates. This exposure exists independently of the application running on PHP.

Additionally, Datadog Security Labs, which independently reproduced the vulnerabilities, found that application-level authentication cannot prevent the attack because PHP processes the malicious request before application code runs. In its reproduction of CVE-2026-109618, researchers reported that the request “never reaches the target application’s code.”

“Even with solid application security practices, your applications could still be exposed because the vulnerable behavior happens below the application, in the PHP runtime itself.”

This means that even with solid application security practices, your applications could still be exposed because the vulnerable behavior happens below the application, in the PHP runtime itself.

The answer is to patch.

The community takes a collaborative effort

Once the full impact became clear in August, the PHP Ecosystem Security Team, the PHP Foundation, and release managers delivered a fix across every supported PHP version. In a cross-ecosystem effort, they also worked with LTS vendors (such as Zend) to ensure they created and released all patches simultaneously.

This is the first time in 20+ years I’ve seen an effort like this happen, and I applaud the community for moving in this direction. Because of this initiative, anyone on a PHP version no longer supported by the community (8.1 or older) could remain secure against these newly disclosed CVEs without any gaps.

Unfortunately, this kind of cooperation also depends on trust, which was tested here. The CVE numbers were leaked on October 20, moving all releases up by a day. But as of 14:00 UTC on October 21, all community-supported PHP versions have received updates to mitigate these vulnerabilities. My team at Zend, along with other LTS providers, also released patches for EOL PHP versions.

While we’ll need more comprehensive steps in the coming weeks, these mitigations will keep critical applications that power governments, hospitals, financial institutions, schools, and more secure and supported in the interim.

AI is changing the economics of vulnerability research

PHP2Shell is a prime example of what happens when AI makes difficult security research more accessible — and the dangers that come with that knowledge.

As part of OpenAI’s Patch the Planet initiative, Calif identified a critical PHP flaw using GPT-5.6 Sol. PHP’s maintainers led the fixes and release, with researchers and security providers contributing testing, technical support, and coordination ahead of disclosure.

“We’ve always raced vulnerability disclosure, patch availability, and exploitation. PHP2Shell demonstrates just how uncomfortable and hard-won that race can, and likely will, become.”

What stands out is the potential shift in scale. OpenAI says these are already among several significant vulnerabilities it has found and is working to address, and it expects similar findings to “increase sharply in the coming months.”

We’ve always raced vulnerability disclosure, patch availability, and exploitation. PHP2Shell demonstrates just how uncomfortable and hard-won that race can, and likely will, become.

Running EOL OSS? AI is raising the stakes.

The easy advice after a vulnerability like PHP2Shell is to upgrade immediately. The operational reality is more complicated.

PHP 8.1 and older releases no longer receive updates from the PHP project, although some distributions and long-term support vendors provide backported security fixes. For critical applications, moving to a new runtime can require updates to frameworks, libraries, extensions, and application code, plus the testing needed to ensure those changes don’t disrupt production.

That gap grows as AI improves vulnerability research, so this isn’t just a PHP issue. PHP is just the first major example of what’s coming for most popular OSS technologies. For instance, we’ve seen a recent flood of Spring vulnerability reports in the past few months, and Node.js and Python reported critical vulnerabilities the same day PHP2Shell landed. I’d also be remiss not to mention Linus Torvalds’ recent comments that the Linux security list is becoming unmanageable because of AI bug reports.

During my time working with OSS and PHP at Perforce Software, I’ve come to view LTS as a bridge to modernization. It lets teams keep addressing security vulnerabilities while they plan, test, and execute a move to a supported version. And, as vulnerability discovery accelerates, remaining indefinitely on unsupported software becomes increasingly difficult to justify.

Organizations need to stay current where they can and have a deliberate security strategy for the systems they can’t upgrade immediately. The faster vulnerabilities are discovered, the more important this will become.

What happens now?

For PHP users, the immediate priority is straightforward: move to a fixed release or obtain appropriate security fixes for an otherwise unsupported version. But let’s talk more long-term.

It can be tempting to use PHP2Shell as evidence that PHP is suddenly less secure, but that couldn’t be further from the truth. The combined community and vendor effort this week proves that. Instead, we need to change our outlook on security, because vulnerabilities like these will only become more common.

“Yes, our capacity to find difficult security problems has improved. But our ability to respond needs to keep pace.”

AI is changing which security investigations are practical and how quickly they can happen. That’s valuable when researchers are working with projects and the wider ecosystem to resolve vulnerabilities. But it also puts more pressure on organizations to know what they’re running, stay on supported releases when possible, establish clear vulnerability-response processes, and have a plan for applications that cannot be upgraded immediately.

Yes, our capacity to find difficult security problems has improved. But our ability to respond needs to keep pace.

The post PHP2Shell was only the beginning: AI is accelerating the patch race appeared first on The New Stack.
AI is accelerating vulnerability discovery. PHP2Shell proves that legacy runtimes can no longer survive without a proactive patch strategy.

item.title: Microsoft’s new voice AI can start working out what you want before you finish speaking
item.dc:creator: Adrian Bridgwater
item.description:
“I think you said, ‘representative.’” It’s the fastest way to bypass automated speech recognition chatbots that fail to route human

The post Microsoft’s new voice AI can start working out what you want before you finish speaking appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
“I think you said, ‘representative.’” It’s the fastest way to bypass automated speech recognition chatbots that fail to route human callers to the service they need. Achieving a human handoff to a living, breathing representative still feels like a badge of honor.

Microsoft wants to change that dynamic.

Naomi Moneypenny, senior director of product development at Microsoft Foundry Models division, blogged on October 1 to introduce three new Microsoft AI (MAI) models in Microsoft Foundry, Redmond’s app and agent model catalog and platform.

“A voice agent has to do more than hear a request and produce a reply. It has to keep the interaction moving while it listens, reasons, uses tools, and speaks. A delay at either end can turn a conversation into a series of awkward pauses,” writes Moneypenny.

Available now in Microsoft Foundry, the latest voice-centric models include MAI-Transcribe-2-Streaming, which turns live speech into text as it is spoken; MAI-Voice-2.1, an expressive multilingual text-to-speech model; and MAI-Voice-2.1-Flash, optimized for responsive, high-volume voice applications.

Partials drive incremental speech recognition

Instead of waiting for a person to finish speaking before returning text, the technology (which has automatic language detection) produces its first hypotheses (known as partials, associated with the field of incremental speech recognition) within the “low hundreds of milliseconds” of receiving audio. The model then refines the partials as more context arrives, before committing to a stable transcript once an utterance ends.

“A live transcription experience can surface words almost as quickly as they are spoken.”

“That distinction matters when an application needs to act while someone is speaking. A customer-service agent can begin identifying a caller’s request before the sentence is complete. A voice assistant can start reasoning or preparing a tool call sooner. A live transcription experience can surface words almost as quickly as they are spoken,” writes Moneypenny. 

MAI-Voice-2.1-Flash is proposed as “a natural fit” for live support agents, voice assistants, and other applications that generate spoken responses. Moneypenny suggests developers can choose MAI-Voice-2.1 when “expressive fidelity” is the priority, or Flash when they need to balance natural speech with responsiveness and cost at scale.

Moneypenny is bullish about the benchmarks thus far. Her post noted that MAI-Transcribe-2-Streaming “debuts at #1 for accuracy” on both partial and final transcripts on the benchmark-based Artificial Analysis leaderboard. 

Time for voice to speak up?

All said and done then (pun intended), does this mean that across the spectrum of human-machine input methods, voice is now ready for wider use and adoption? CEO of voice-agent platform company Phonely, Will Bodewes, tells The New Stack he sees these developments positively.

“Voice AI is ready for prime time, if Microsoft’s entry into the market is any indication,” Bodewes says.

Microsoft is hardly new to speech, though: Azure Speech has been on the market for years, and it ships the new MAI models. “For an AI developer, that’s an opportunity to build on that momentum, so expect more players to follow suit. But the model is only the beginning. Voice agents need to learn from every call and measurably improve over time. For companies to see real results, their voice AI must be ready for prime time in theory and in practice.”

“In the early days, a speech request to a hosted model could sit behind a thousand others for 30 seconds, which, on a phone call, is a hang-up.”

From an infrastructure-operations perspective, there’s a clear advancement here. Bodewes, whose company builds its own voice-agent LLM, notes that in the early days (and he means back from the mid 2010s onwards in the initial cloud-based speech API era, such as the Google Cloud Speech-to-Text API, Azure Speech Services, Amazon Transcribe, etc.) a speech request to a hosted model could sit behind a thousand others for 30 seconds, which, on a phone call, is a hang-up. 

“We built routing infrastructure just to find the least-loaded endpoints. Owning the model meant owning the queue, and that’s how we got to 120-millisecond responses,” explains Bodewes. “Every sentence you add to a prompt adds another chance of failure. So we enforce the critical steps in code. If an agent needs a name, email, and date of birth before it issues a refund, the codebase guarantees it. Leaving that to the LLM is how you ship incidents.”

The front end (speech) isn’t the hard part

Phonely machine learning researcher Amit Kiran Rege tells The New Stack he agrees the developments are positive, but warns of deeper nuances (speech pun intended, again) in the wider rollout. 

“Microsoft shipped the two ends of the voice agent pipeline, speech in and speech out, which tells you it’s betting on a cascade effect for contact centers, the same as we did. But in our work, we found the ends aren’t the hard part. The hard part is the silence in the middle where the model is deciding whether a caller is done or taking a breath before the next word,” explains Rege.

What surprised Phonely when scaling this type of service to millions of calls is that speeding up the data pipeline makes the agent interrupt callers more. 

“Microsoft shipped the two ends of the voice agent pipeline, speech in and speech out … But in our work, we found the ends aren’t the hard part.”

“Two-thirds of the time our agent decided to jump in too early, and nobody heard it, because the caller resumed before the first syllable and we canceled the reply. Cut your latency in half, and those become audible interruptions. Thus, the lesson is that latency and turn-taking have to improve together,” cautions Rege.

Talking our way into future interfaces

Microsoft’s position on these technologies states that developers can embrace these same models and toolsets to build customer-service agents, multilingual assistants that recognize a spoken language and reply in a consistent voice, what it defines as “interactive learning experiences that move between languages, speakers, and conversational exercises” and live captions and voice-driven interfaces.

The post Microsoft’s new voice AI can start working out what you want before you finish speaking appeared first on The New Stack.
Microsoft’s speech model starts transcribing before callers finish talking. But Phonely says the hard part of voice AI is the silence in the middle.

item.title: Five AI agent harnesses took the same memory test. The results weren’t even close.
item.dc:creator: Amanda Caswell
item.description:
AI agents are getting better at remembering past conversations and earlier tasks but remembering something doesn’t guarantee an agent can

The post Five AI agent harnesses took the same memory test. The results weren’t even close. appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
AI agents are getting better at remembering past conversations and earlier tasks but remembering something doesn’t guarantee an agent can use it to do better work next time. Letta’s new FrontierMemory benchmark, released Wednesday, tests that gap by measuring whether agents can learn from experience rather than by just retrieving stored information.
